title: How You Buy the Building Decides Who Carries Its Risks
summary: Procurement is the set of choices about how design and construction are bought: who designs, who builds, when the price is fixed and who carries what. This lesson compares design-bid-build, design-build, construction manager at risk and construction manager as agent, maps them to the FIDIC Red, Yellow and Silver forms, and walks through prequalification, bid levelling, buyout and the guaranteed maximum price.
body:
There is no best delivery method, only a best match between the risks you want to keep, the risks a contractor can genuinely carry, and how mature your design is when you buy. Choose the method first, then the contract form, then the contractor.

Recall

Q. Under a fixed or stipulated price, who generally carries rising material costs?

A. The contractor, who prices that risk into its bid, unless the contract includes a price adjustment clause. The risk returns to the owner if the contractor cannot absorb it.

Q. What is the critical path?

A. The longest chain of dependent activities through the schedule; any delay to an activity on it delays the finish date.

Q. What is a tornado chart?

A. A chart that ranks inputs by how much a plausible change in each moves a chosen result, such as profit or return, so the longest bars show where risk is concentrated.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in Week 51 Quincy taught you to forecast cost honestly. That forecast depends on a decision made earlier: how you bought the work. The same building, bought two different ways, carries different prices, different speeds and different arguments. A developer who signs a contract form because his contractor suggested it has let the other side of the table choose who carries the risk.

The four delivery methods

Design-bid-build is the traditional sequence. You hire a designer, complete the drawings, invite contractors to bid on them, and award a construction contract, usually at a fixed price. Its strength is a clear, competitive price on a complete design. Its weakness is time, because construction cannot start until design is finished, and the fact that the owner warrants the design to the contractor, so every error in the drawings becomes the owner's change order.

Design-build puts design and construction in one contract with one firm. You define requirements; the design-builder designs and builds them, often for a fixed price. It is usually faster and gives you one party responsible for both. The cost is control: you are buying a performance, not a drawing, so a loose brief produces a building you did not intend at a price you cannot challenge.

Construction manager at risk brings a builder in during design. It advises on cost, buildability and sequence, then commits to a guaranteed maximum price, a cap on the cost of the work plus its fee, usually when design is far enough along to price. It then buys the trade packages, often openly, and carries overruns above the cap except for owner changes. Construction manager as agent is an adviser only: it manages the trades, but you hold the trade contracts and you carry the cost risk.

Applied example, hypothetical. A developer with a 30-month programme and a lender requiring a firm price at closing. Design-bid-build gives a firm price but adds months of design before construction. Construction manager as agent is fast and flexible but gives the lender no cap. Design-build gives a cap early but on a brief, not a design. Construction manager at risk, with the guaranteed maximum price set at about 80 to 90 percent design completion, often fits this case: earlier start than design-bid-build, a cap the lender can rely on, and design control kept with the owner. That percentage is practitioner habit, not a standard.

Mapping to the FIDIC forms

Internationally, many projects, particularly those funded by development lenders, use the standard forms published by FIDIC, the international federation of consulting engineers. In broad terms, the Red Book is for construction designed by the employer, usually paid against measured quantities, and is closest to design-bid-build. The Yellow Book is for plant and design-build, where the contractor designs to the employer's requirements. The Silver Book is for engineering, procurement and construction, sometimes called turnkey, where the contractor takes most of the design and ground risk for a fixed price. FIDIC states which form it intends for which situation; verify against the current editions before you choose one.

Say that out loud now.

Red, the owner designs. Yellow, the contractor designs. Silver, the contractor designs and carries almost everything, and prices it accordingly.

Prequalification, bid levelling and buyout

Prequalification screens contractors before they bid: financial strength, bonding capacity, safety record, similar work, key staff and claims history. Its purpose is to make sure every bid you receive comes from a firm you would actually hire, so the lowest price is a real option.

Bid levelling puts bids on the same basis before comparing them. Bidders exclude different items, qualify different assumptions and price different alternates. You add the cost of each exclusion, remove items that are not in scope and price each qualification, so that you compare complete prices. Day 5 works a full example.

Buyout is the process of awarding the trade packages and converting estimates into commitments. Under a guaranteed maximum price, you should see every trade bid and every levelling sheet, because buyout is where the contractor's contingency is either preserved or consumed.

One warning about the guaranteed maximum price. Its real content is not the headline number but the list of assumptions and clarifications attached to it. A cap set too early, on a design that is still moving, arrives with dozens of clarifications, each one a future change order. Read that list as carefully as the price. A short list on a mature design is a cap; a long list on an early design is an estimate wearing a cap's name.

How the best do it

The most disciplined owners decide the delivery method by a written risk allocation before they talk to any contractor: a table listing each major risk, such as design errors, ground, price escalation, weather, permits and subcontractor default, and who is best placed to carry it. Only then do they choose the method and form that puts each risk there. A small developer can copy this with one page and ten rows. If the table says you want to keep design control and transfer price risk, the method almost chooses itself.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how the contract price is split between design services and construction can affect indirect tax and the tax treatment of costs; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: under design-bid-build you warrant the design; under design-build the contractor does, so your professional indemnity needs change. Banking: lenders usually want a firm price or a guaranteed maximum price before first draw. Governance: record the risk allocation decision and who approved it. Estate: if your guarantees sit behind a cost-reimbursable contract, your estate's exposure is larger than under a fixed price. Exit: a buyer will ask who warrants the design and for how long; the delivery method answers that.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on the contract form and amendments; cost consultant, on the guaranteed maximum price build-up.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a method that transfers a risk to a party that cannot carry it, or fixing a price on a design too immature to price. The control is the written risk allocation table, prequalification that tests financial capacity, and a design-maturity check before any price is fixed.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner awards to the lowest headline bid. The lowest levelled bid from a prequalified firm is the only number worth comparing.

Callback

In Week 49, Marco and Quincy built the work breakdown structure and the schedule of values. Procurement is where those tools earn their keep: each bid package is a branch of the work breakdown structure, and the levelling sheet is a schedule of values written in advance, so every bidder prices the same scope against the same lines.

Recap

Design-bid-build fixes a price on a finished design; design-build buys design and construction together; construction manager at risk adds early advice and a guaranteed maximum price; construction manager as agent advises while you carry cost. FIDIC's Red, Yellow and Silver books map roughly to who designs and who carries risk. Prequalify, level the bids, and watch buyout.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Wembley Stadium and the fixed price that did not make the risk disappear.
checklist: I have a written risk allocation table before choosing a delivery method.
I match the delivery method to my design maturity and my lender's need for price certainty.
I know which FIDIC form, if any, fits my design responsibility.
Every bidder is prequalified on finances, bonding, safety and similar work.
I compare levelled bids, never headline bids.
Under a guaranteed maximum price, I see every trade bid and levelling sheet.
A construction lawyer has reviewed the contract form and amendments.
head: Field checklist
speak: How I buy the building decides who carries its risks. Design-bid-build gives a competitive fixed price on a finished design, but it is slow and I warrant the design. Design-build puts design and construction with one firm, faster, but I am buying a performance against a brief, so the brief must be tight. Construction manager at risk brings a builder in during design, then commits to a guaranteed maximum price, a cap on cost plus fee, while I keep design control. Construction manager as agent advises, but I hold the trade contracts and the cost risk. Internationally, FIDIC's Red Book suits an owner's design, the Yellow Book a contractor's design, and the Silver Book a turnkey deal where the contractor carries almost everything at a price. Before any of that, I write a risk allocation table. Then I prequalify bidders, level their bids to the same scope, and watch buyout.
terms: Guaranteed maximum price — a cap on the cost of the work plus the contractor's fee, above which the contractor pays, except for owner-approved changes.
Construction manager at risk — a delivery method in which a builder advises during design, then commits to a guaranteed maximum price and holds the trade contracts.
Bid levelling — adjusting competing bids for exclusions, qualifications and scope differences so they can be compared on the same basis.

hostile.q: Why are you using construction manager at risk instead of hard-bidding a fixed price? Isn't a guaranteed maximum price just a cost-plus contract with a promise attached?
hostile.a: It is a cap, and the cap is only as good as the design behind it. We chose it because it lets us start the structure earlier while keeping design control and giving you a firm ceiling at closing. The price will be set at about 85 percent design, the contractor's contingency has written rules, we see every trade bid, and our own contingency sits outside the contract. If the design were complete, I would hard-bid it.

title: Wembley Stadium: The Fixed Price That Did Not Make the Risk Disappear
summary: The rebuilding of Wembley Stadium in London was let as a fixed-price design-and-build contract in 2002, ran late, cost the contractor heavily and led to long disputes, while the owner lost a season of major events. Ford and Cole take the procurement story through seven forensic steps and ask what a fixed price really transfers.
body:
At Wembley the owner bought certainty of price and still paid in time, events and years of dispute, because a fixed price moves the cost of a problem to the contractor but leaves the consequences of the problem on the owner's calendar.

Recall

Q. What does a to-complete performance index above 1.0 tell you?

A. That the remaining work must be done more cost-efficiently than planned in order to finish on the target budget. If the project has been running below 1.0, a plan that needs well above 1.0 is a hope.

Q. In a Last Planner approach, what is a reliable weekly commitment?

A. A promise by the crew that will do the work, made only when the work is sound: its prerequisites, information, materials and space are in place. The percentage of promises kept is tracked every week.

Q. In the Dubai World case of 2009, what was the shock that markets reacted to?

A. A request for a standstill on debt repayments by a state-linked development group, which showed lenders that implicit state support could not be assumed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this case is as much about contract as about construction. You will be offered fixed prices by contractors who want your project. Every one of them is a promise that someone else will absorb a problem. This case asks what happens when the problem is larger than the promise.

A note on facts. The rebuilding of Wembley Stadium is real and publicly documented. The broad sequence below is well reported; I deliberately use no cost or loss figures, because published figures vary with what is counted. Treat interpretive points as my analysis, and verify specifics against the published court judgments and reports before you rely on them.

1. Timeline

The national stadium's owner chose to demolish the old Wembley and build a new stadium with a large steel arch. In 2002 it signed a design-and-build contract with Multiplex, an Australian contractor, at a fixed price. Steelwork for the roof and arch was subcontracted. In 2004 the steelwork subcontractor, Cleveland Bridge, left the project after disputes with Multiplex, and replacement steel contractors were brought in. The stadium had been expected to host the 2006 FA Cup Final; that match was moved to Cardiff when completion slipped. The stadium was finished and opened in 2007. Litigation followed between Multiplex and the steel subcontractor, and other disputes ran on for years after opening.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the outcome. The owner's choice of a fixed-price design-and-build contract for a structurally ambitious, one-off building. The contractor's acceptance of a fixed price for that risk. And the contractor's subcontracting of the most complex package, the steel arch and roof, where a dispute in one subcontract could stop the critical path.

3. Assumptions

The owner assumed that a fixed price meant price risk had been transferred and therefore did not need managing. The contractor assumed that its price would hold for a design it was still developing. Both assumed the steel package would be bought and built as planned. None of those assumptions is unreasonable alone. Together they put a one-of-a-kind structure on a fixed price with its riskiest element one contract removed from the party carrying the risk.

4. Incentives

A contractor bidding a fixed price for a prestigious project has an incentive to win it and to treat risk optimistically. Once losses appear, its incentive changes: to recover them through claims against the owner and its subcontractors, and to protect cash. A subcontractor in dispute with a main contractor has an incentive to stop work rather than finance it. The owner, having fixed the price, had an incentive to treat cost as someone else's problem, which can make an owner slow to see that a contractor's losses will soon become the owner's delay.

Say that out loud now.

A fixed price moves the cost of a problem. It does not move the problem off my calendar.

5. Warning signs ignored

A fixed price for a structure with few precedents. Design still being developed by the contractor after the price was fixed. A dispute in the steel subcontract, the package on the critical path, years before completion. Public reports of the contractor's mounting losses. Each of these is a sign that the party carrying the risk may not be able, or willing, to carry it quietly.

6. Point of no return

For the owner's programme, the point of no return was the steel subcontractor's departure in 2004. Replacing the most complex package mid-stream on a structure of that kind made the original completion date very hard to keep. After that, the question was not whether events would be lost but how many, and who would pay for the delay.

7. Root cause

The root cause was treating a fixed price as a transfer of risk rather than as a transfer of the cost of risk. On a unique, complex structure with a developing design, the risk was real and large. Pricing it fixed did not make it smaller. It concentrated it in a contractor whose losses then drove disputes, and in a subcontract chain where one break stopped the job.

Cole's view: what the contract can and cannot do

A fixed-price contract can say who pays for overruns. It can set liquidated damages, a pre-agreed sum per day of delay. What it cannot do is deliver your opening date. Liquidated damages are usually capped and are often far below the owner's real loss, such as lost events and revenue, and they are only worth what the contractor can pay. An owner who relies on the contract alone has bought a claim, not a building on time. The protections that matter are earlier: prequalification that tests whether the contractor can survive the risk, a requirement to approve key subcontractors, step-in rights over critical subcontracts, security such as bonds, and design maturity before the price is fixed.

What a different procurement might have looked like

This is analysis, not a verdict on the parties. For a one-off structure, an owner has alternatives to a single fixed price. A two-stage approach brings the contractor in early to develop the design and price the risky packages openly, and fixes the price only once the most uncertain elements, such as the arch and roof, are designed and bought. The owner can also procure or pre-qualify the critical specialist directly and assign it to the main contractor, so the most important subcontract is chosen for capability rather than price. Each costs some certainty early in exchange for fewer surprises late.

The prevention

Rule 52: Never treat a fixed price as risk gone; award it only to a contractor whose finances can carry the risk transferred, on a design mature enough to price, with approval and step-in rights over the critical subcontracts.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a fixed price that is larger than the contractor's capacity to lose money. The control is prequalification on finances and bonding, a design-maturity test before fixing the price, and contract rights over key subcontracts.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner celebrates a contractor's fixed price as if it were an insurance policy. It is a promise backed only by that contractor's balance sheet and its security.

Callback

In Week 40, Ford and Roman took a composite case where a contractor's insolvency became the developer's guarantee call. Wembley is the reverse direction of the same lesson: the owner did not carry the overrun, but it still carried the delay. Whether a contractor fails outright or fights its losses, the owner's timeline pays.

Recap

Wembley was let as a fixed-price design-and-build contract in 2002; its critical steel subcontract broke down in 2004; the 2006 FA Cup Final went to Cardiff; the stadium opened in 2007; disputes followed. The fixed price moved cost, not consequences.

Rule 52: Never treat a fixed price as risk gone; award it only to a contractor whose finances can carry the risk transferred, on a design mature enough to price, with approval and step-in rights over the critical subcontracts.

Next: Priya on The Money: what each delivery method does to price, speed, interest cost and the lender's view.
checklist: I test whether the contractor's balance sheet can carry the risk a fixed price transfers.
I fix a price only on a design mature enough to price.
I approve the subcontractors for packages on the critical path.
My contract gives me step-in rights over critical subcontracts.
I hold security, such as a performance bond, sized to the risk transferred.
I compare liquidated damages with my real cost of delay.
I treat public reports of contractor losses as a warning sign.
head: Field checklist
speak: The rebuilding of Wembley Stadium in London was let in 2002 as a fixed-price design-and-build contract with Multiplex, for a structurally ambitious stadium with a great steel arch. The steel subcontractor, Cleveland Bridge, left in 2004 after disputes, the 2006 FA Cup Final had to move to Cardiff, the stadium opened in 2007, and years of disputes followed. The owner had bought price certainty, but it still paid in lost events and lost time. The root cause was treating a fixed price as a transfer of risk rather than a transfer of the cost of risk. On a unique structure with a developing design, the risk stayed large and simply concentrated in a contractor whose losses drove disputes. Liquidated damages are capped and only worth what the contractor can pay. Rule 52: never treat a fixed price as risk gone; award it only to a contractor who can carry it, on a mature design, with rights over the critical subcontracts.
terms: Liquidated damages — a sum agreed in the contract, often per day, payable by the contractor for late completion instead of proving actual loss.
Step-in rights — a contract right allowing the owner or its nominee to take over a subcontract if the main contractor fails or defaults.
Design maturity — how complete and stable the design is when a price is fixed, which decides how much of the price is still a guess.

hostile.q: You have a fixed-price contract. Why do you need a bond, step-in rights and subcontractor approval as well? Aren't you paying twice for the same protection?
hostile.a: No. The fixed price allocates the cost of overruns. It does nothing for my opening date or for a contractor that cannot pay. Liquidated damages are capped and only as good as the contractor's balance sheet. The bond gives me a solvent party if the contractor fails, step-in rights keep the critical steel moving if a subcontract breaks, and approval keeps an untested firm off the critical path. Each protects a different failure.

rule: Rule 52: Never treat a fixed price as risk gone; award it only to a contractor whose finances can carry the risk transferred, on a design mature enough to price, with approval and step-in rights over the critical subcontracts.

title: Price Certainty, Speed and Interest: What the Delivery Method Costs
summary: Every delivery method trades price certainty against speed and control, and each of those has a dollar value. This lesson prices them on a hypothetical project: the risk premium inside a fixed price, the fees and general conditions under a construction manager, and the interest and lost income that a faster start or a later finish move. It ends with Warrick's Wealth Ledger.
body:
A fixed price is not cheaper or dearer than a construction manager's guaranteed maximum price; it buys something different. The way to choose is to put a dollar value on certainty and a dollar value on time, and on most development loans time is the larger number.

Recall

Q. In a cost meeting, why state the overrun in dollars rather than as a percentage?

A. Because a dollar figure sounds like an honest report and lets the lender test it immediately, while a vague percentage or "a modest variance" sounds like spin.

Q. What does one month of delay cost at the end of construction?

A. Interest on a loan that is almost fully drawn, extended overheads, and a month of stabilised income that has not started, so the last month is usually the most expensive one.

Q. In a stress test, what is a severe case for?

A. To show what happens when several bad inputs arrive together, and to plan the response before it is needed, not to predict the future.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Marco taught the methods and Ford showed that a fixed price does not remove risk. Today I put numbers on the choice, because your lender, your investors and your own returns all react to it. The same building, bought two ways, can differ by more than a million dollars before a single change order is signed.

What is inside each price

Under a fixed price, the contractor's bid includes its estimate of the work, its overheads and profit, and a risk premium: money for the risks it is taking on, such as price escalation, design gaps and ground. You never see that premium as a line, but it is there, and it is larger when the design is less complete or the market is busy.

Under construction manager at risk, you see the parts. The cost of the work is the trade packages; general conditions are the contractor's site costs, such as supervision, site offices and temporary works; the fee is a percentage of cost, covering head-office overhead and profit; and the contractor's contingency sits inside the cap. Fee percentages and contingency sizes are commercial practice, negotiated, not standards.

Hypothetical example. Hard cost of the work is 25,000,000 dollars. A fixed-price bid might include a 3 percent risk premium, 750,000 dollars, hidden inside the price. A construction manager's guaranteed maximum price might show a 3 percent fee, 750,000 dollars, general conditions of 1,500,000 dollars and a contractor's contingency of 750,000 dollars. On paper they look similar. The difference is that unused contingency under the cap may come back to you, depending on the contract, while the fixed-price premium never does, and that under the cap you carry more of the cost of any risk that falls outside the contractor's contingency.

Time is usually the bigger number

Design-bid-build waits for design to finish before construction starts. Construction manager at risk or design-build can overlap them. Suppose the overlap starts construction six months earlier and the building opens six months earlier.

Hypothetical: a construction loan of 20,000,000 dollars at 7 percent interest a year, nearly fully drawn at the end of construction. One month of interest at that balance is 20,000,000 times 0.07 divided by 12, about 116,667 dollars. The stabilised building earns net operating income of 1,500,000 dollars a year, which is 125,000 dollars a month. So each month at the end costs roughly 116,667 plus 125,000, about 241,667 dollars, before extended overheads. Six months is about 1,450,000 dollars.

Compare that with the 750,000 dollar risk premium. On these numbers, the faster method is worth roughly twice the fixed-price premium, even before any change orders, provided the guaranteed maximum price is set on a mature enough design that clarifications do not eat the saving. That proviso is not a footnote. Rule 52 still applies.

Say that out loud now.

A month at the end costs interest plus income I have not started earning. On most loans, time is worth more than the premium for certainty.

How the fee is written changes behaviour

A fee stated as a percentage of the cost of the work rises when cost rises. That is a small but real incentive pointing the wrong way: the contractor earns more on a change order than on a saving. Many owners therefore convert the fee to a fixed amount once the guaranteed maximum price is agreed, adjusted only for owner-approved changes in scope. Some add an incentive: a share of any savings below the cap, or a bonus for finishing early. Each structure is commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal, not a standard.

Hypothetical: on the 25,000,000 dollar cost above, a 3 percent fee is 750,000 dollars. If cost grows by 1,000,000 dollars through changes, a percentage fee grows by 30,000 dollars; a fixed fee does not. The amount is small. The signal is not. Write the fee so that the contractor earns more by buying well and finishing on time, not by spending more.

What the lender sees

A construction lender wants a firm cost before first draw, because its in-balance test needs a reliable cost to complete. A fixed price from a strong contractor gives that directly. A guaranteed maximum price gives it if the cap is set before closing and the clarifications are short. Construction manager as agent gives no cap at all, so a lender will usually require more equity, a larger owner's contingency or a stronger cost-overrun guarantee to compensate. Under design-build, the lender will look hard at the employer's requirements, because a loose brief makes the fixed price less firm than it looks.

Bid levelling also has a money value. A headline bid that is 200,000 dollars lower but excludes 300,000 dollars of work is 100,000 dollars dearer. Day 5 works this through. The lender's monitor will level the bids whether you do or not.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick's point for your personal balance sheet is about where residual risk lands. Under a fixed price from a strong contractor, much of the cost risk sits with the contractor and its surety. Under a construction manager as agent, it sits with the owner, and through any cost-overrun guarantee, with you personally. Before you choose a method for its speed, ask what it does to the size of the personal guarantee the lender will ask for, and whether your liquidity floor can carry that guarantee being called. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financing decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a faster method for its time saving and then losing the saving to clarifications, allowances and changes because the price was fixed too early. The control is to model time and cost together, set the cap only on a design mature enough to price, and track clarifications as a cost line.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares the fee percentage of two construction managers and picks the lower one. Compare the whole cap: fee, general conditions, contingency and the length of the clarifications list. A low fee with high general conditions is not cheaper.

Callback

In Week 51, Nadia showed that because the loan is fixed, an overrun lands almost entirely on equity. Delivery method decides how much of that overrun risk you keep. A method that keeps more risk with the owner needs a larger owner's contingency, and on Nadia's arithmetic, every dollar of overrun beyond it is a dollar of your equity.

Recap

A fixed price hides a risk premium; a guaranteed maximum price shows fee, general conditions and contingency. Time is usually worth more: on hypothetical numbers, each month at the end cost about 241,667 dollars, so six months was worth about twice the fixed-price premium. The lender wants a firm cost, and the method you choose sets the size of your personal guarantee.

Next: LEX on The Rules: tender law, the duty of fairness in bidding, and how the FIDIC forms allocate risk.
checklist: I estimate the risk premium inside any fixed price I am offered.
I compare whole guaranteed maximum prices: fee, general conditions, contingency and clarifications.
I price one month of delay at the end of construction: interest plus lost income.
I model time and cost together before choosing a delivery method.
I know what my lender requires for each delivery method before first draw.
I track clarifications to a guaranteed maximum price as a cost line.
I know how the delivery method changes the personal guarantee I will be asked for.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every delivery method trades certainty against speed, and both have a price. A fixed price hides a risk premium, perhaps 3 percent, inside the bid. A construction manager's guaranteed maximum price shows the parts: cost of the work, general conditions, a fee and the contractor's contingency, some of which may come back to me. Time is usually the bigger number. On a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar loan at 7 percent, a month at the end costs about 116,667 dollars in interest, plus 125,000 dollars of income not yet earned: about 241,667 dollars a month. Six months is about 1,450,000 dollars, roughly twice a 750,000 dollar risk premium. But the saving only holds if the cap is set on a mature design with a short clarifications list. The lender wants a firm cost before first draw, and the less risk the contractor carries, the larger the guarantee the lender will ask me for.
terms: Risk premium — the amount a contractor adds to a fixed price to cover the risks it is taking on, not shown as a separate line.
General conditions — the contractor's site-related costs, such as supervision, site offices, temporary facilities and equipment, priced separately from trade work.
Clarifications — the list of assumptions and exclusions attached to a guaranteed maximum price, each of which can become a change.

hostile.q: Your construction manager's fee is 1 percent higher than the other bidder's. Why are you paying more?
hostile.a: Because the fee is the smallest part of the cap. Levelled on the whole price, the other bidder's general conditions are 400,000 dollars higher, its contingency is thinner, and its clarifications list is twice as long. Our choice is lower on the full guaranteed maximum price and carries fewer future changes. I will send you the levelling sheet so you can test that line by line.

title: Tender Law and the Standard Forms: What Binds When You Invite Bids
summary: Inviting bids is not legally neutral. In some common law systems, notably Canada, an invitation to tender can create a contract with each compliant bidder that obliges the owner to treat them fairly. This lesson covers that idea, the owner's duties when evaluating bids, and how the FIDIC Red, Yellow and Silver books and a guaranteed maximum price contract allocate design and ground risk.
body:
The moment you invite formal bids, you may owe the bidders duties you did not intend: to follow your own rules, to evaluate fairly and not to accept a non-compliant bid. Write the tender documents as carefully as the contract, because in some jurisdictions they are a contract.

Recall

Q. State Rule 51.

A. Report the forecast final cost, in the dollars you will actually pay, every month to the people funding the project, and never let a published estimate leave out a cost you know you will pay.

Q. Why should a contract require prompt written notice of delay?

A. So that the owner learns of a delay while it can still be mitigated, and so that a later claim is tied to a dated record rather than a reconstruction. Many contracts make the notice a condition of any extension.

Q. What is a financial covenant in a loan?

A. A promise by the borrower to keep a measure, such as debt service coverage or loan to value, within a stated limit, tested on stated dates, with consequences if it is breached.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Marco taught the methods and Priya priced them. Today is about the legal machinery of buying. Owners lose disputes they never expected because they treated a tender as an informal shopping exercise, rejected a low bidder for an unstated reason, or quietly negotiated with one bidder after the deadline. Each of those can be a breach.

Contract A and Contract B

In plain English: in Canada, the courts have held that a formal call for tenders can create a preliminary contract, called Contract A, between the owner and each bidder who submits a compliant bid. The construction contract that follows with the winner is Contract B. The leading case is The Queen against Ron Engineering, decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1981. It concerned a bidder that made an arithmetic mistake and tried to withdraw; the court held that the bid could not simply be withdrawn, because submitting it formed Contract A.

Later Canadian cases built duties onto Contract A. In M.J.B. Enterprises against Defence Construction, decided in 1999, the Supreme Court of Canada held that an owner could not accept a non-compliant bid, even though the tender documents said the lowest bid would not necessarily be accepted. In Tercon Contractors against British Columbia, decided in 2010, the owner had accepted a bid from an ineligible bidder, and the court considered whether an exclusion clause protected the owner. These are Canadian authorities; other common law systems approach tendering differently, and the details matter. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The practical lesson is the same everywhere: if you write rules for a competition, follow them, or write rules that preserve the flexibility you need.

Say that out loud now.

If I write rules for a tender, I follow them. If I need flexibility, I write it in before the bids arrive.

What the tender documents should say

Say what is being priced, by reference to drawings, specifications and a bid form with fixed lines. Say what makes a bid compliant: deadline, format, security, required forms. Say how bids will be evaluated, including whether price alone decides or whether price and quality are weighed, and with what weights. Say what rights you reserve: to reject all bids, to waive minor irregularities, to negotiate with the preferred bidder, and to cancel. And say whether bidders may withdraw before award, and for how long their prices must stay open.

Applied example, hypothetical. You invite five prequalified contractors to bid a 10,000,000 dollar package, stating that the lowest compliant bid will be accepted. The lowest bid omits a required bond form. If you accept it anyway because the price is good, a Canadian court applying M.J.B. might find you breached Contract A with the second bidder, whose damages could include its lost profit. If instead your documents had reserved the right to waive minor irregularities, and the omission was genuinely minor, your position would be stronger. The difference is a sentence written before bidding.

How the standard forms allocate design and ground risk

The FIDIC forms allocate risk differently, and the differences track the delivery method. Under the Red Book, the employer provides the design, so design errors are generally the employer's risk, and the contract includes a mechanism for the contractor to recover for physical conditions that an experienced contractor could not reasonably have foreseen. Under the Yellow Book, the contractor designs to the employer's requirements, and those requirements become the central document, often with a fitness-for-purpose obligation. Under the Silver Book, the contractor carries most of the design risk and, broadly, much more of the ground risk, which is why it is generally intended for projects where the contractor has the time and access to investigate the site. Verify against the current editions' wording before you rely on any of this.

A guaranteed maximum price contract, such as those in the American Institute of Architects family of forms for a construction manager as constructor, turns on a few definitions: what counts as the cost of the work, what the fee covers, what the contractor's contingency may be used for, what happens to savings and what records the owner may audit. Read those definitions before the cap. A broad definition of reimbursable cost can make a cap meaningless.

Subcontractor bids and bid shopping

Tender law has a second layer. When a general contractor bids your job, it relies on prices from subcontractors, often received minutes before your deadline. Bid shopping is the practice of using one subcontractor's price to force another to cut theirs after the main bid has been won. It is legal in some places, restricted in others, and widely regarded in the industry as corrosive, because subcontractors who expect to be shopped pad their first price. Some markets use a bid depository, a system that collects trade bids under rules about timing and confidentiality, to limit it. Whether one applies to your project is a local question; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

As owner, you can reduce the practice directly. Require the general contractor to name its key subcontractors with its bid, and say whether and how they may be substituted afterwards. A named list protects you from a winning bid built on a subcontractor price that will never be honoured, and protects the honest subcontractors who priced your job properly.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on the tender documents and the contract form before any invitation is issued.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is running a formal tender informally: shifting evaluation criteria, negotiating privately with one bidder, or accepting a non-compliant bid. The control is tender documents that state the rules and reserved rights clearly, a written evaluation against those rules, and legal review before award.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner shops the lowest bid to the preferred contractor and asks it to match. Beyond the legal risk in some systems, it teaches the market that your tenders are not real, and the best contractors stop bidding them.

Callback

In Week 20, I taught that the label on a document does not decide whether it binds; its terms and the parties' conduct do. Contract A is the sharpest example: an owner who thought it was only asking for prices found it had made a promise to every compliant bidder.

Recap

In Canada, a formal tender can create Contract A with each compliant bidder, as Ron Engineering held in 1981, carrying duties such as not accepting a non-compliant bid, as in M.J.B. in 1999. Write clear rules and reserved rights, and follow them. FIDIC's Red, Yellow and Silver books shift design and ground risk progressively to the contractor. In a guaranteed maximum price contract, the definitions decide the cap.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: working backward from a target guaranteed maximum price, and levelling three real-looking bids.
checklist: My tender documents state what makes a bid compliant.
My tender documents state how bids will be evaluated and with what weights.
I reserve, in writing, the rights I may need: to reject all bids, waive minor irregularities and negotiate.
I never accept a bid that does not comply with my own rules.
I do not shop one bidder's price to another.
I read the cost-of-the-work definition before the guaranteed maximum price.
A construction lawyer reviews the tender documents before they are issued.
head: Field checklist
speak: Inviting formal bids is not legally neutral. In Canada, the Supreme Court held in Ron Engineering, in 1981, that a call for tenders can create a preliminary contract, Contract A, with every compliant bidder, before the construction contract, Contract B, is signed. Later cases added duties: in M.J.B. Enterprises in 1999, an owner could not accept a non-compliant bid even though it had said the lowest bid would not necessarily be accepted. Other systems differ, so I verify against the primary source. The practical rule is universal: write clear tender rules, state the evaluation method and reserve the rights I need, and then follow them. In the FIDIC forms, design and ground risk shift toward the contractor as I move from the Red Book to the Yellow to the Silver. And in a guaranteed maximum price contract, the definition of the cost of the work decides whether the cap means anything.
terms: Contract A — in Canadian tender law, the preliminary contract formed between an owner and each compliant bidder when a formal tender is submitted.
Compliant bid — a bid that meets the mandatory requirements stated in the tender documents, such as deadline, form and security.
Fitness for purpose — a contractor's obligation that the finished work will be suitable for the purpose stated, which is stricter than an obligation to use reasonable skill and care.

hostile.q: Your lowest bidder forgot to include its bond form. Its price is 300,000 dollars below the next bid. Why not just accept it and ask for the bond later?
hostile.a: Because our tender said a bond form was mandatory, and in some jurisdictions accepting a non-compliant bid can be a breach owed to the compliant bidders, with the next bidder's lost profit as damages. I will ask counsel whether our reserved right to waive minor irregularities covers this omission. If it does not, we award to the lowest compliant bid, and next time we decide which requirements are truly mandatory before we issue the tender.

title: Working Backward from the Cap: Trade Budget and a Levelled Bid
summary: A reverse-engineering calculation. Starting from a hypothetical guaranteed maximum price of 15,900,000 dollars that the pro forma can afford, the lesson strips out fee, insurance, general conditions and contingency to find the most the trade packages may cost. Then it levels three bids for one package and shows that the lowest headline bid is not the lowest real price.
body:
If your pro forma can afford a guaranteed maximum price of 15,900,000 dollars, work backward and you find the trade packages must be bought for no more than 13,000,000 dollars. Then level every bid, because the cheapest number on the tabulation is often not the cheapest price.

Recall

Q. Under construction manager as agent, who carries the cost risk?

A. The owner, who holds the trade contracts directly; the construction manager advises and manages but does not guarantee a price.

Q. In a forward and backward pass of a schedule, what does the backward pass give you?

A. The latest start and finish dates each activity can have without delaying the project; comparing them with the earliest dates gives float.

Q. What is a break-even cost?

A. The total cost at which a chosen result just reaches its limit, for example where profit falls to zero or the development spread disappears.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a contractor will tell you what your building costs. Your pro forma tells you what it can afford. Reverse engineering connects the two before buyout, so you know the trade budget you are defending, and bid levelling makes sure each package is compared on the same scope. This is how you keep a guaranteed maximum price honest from the owner's side of the table.

Step 1: the finished outcome

Hypothetical. The pro forma, with its required return, can afford a guaranteed maximum price of 15,900,000 dollars for the work. The construction manager's proposal states: fee 4 percent of cost; insurance and bond 2 percent of cost; general conditions a fixed 1,480,000 dollars; contractor's contingency 4 percent of trade cost. All of these percentages are commercial terms negotiated on this hypothetical deal, not standards.

Step 2: remove the percentages charged on cost

Fee and insurance together are 4 plus 2, or 6 percent of the cost beneath them. So the cap equals that cost times 1.06. Working backward: 15,900,000 dollars divided by 1.06 equals 15,000,000 dollars. Check forward: 15,000,000 times 0.06 is 900,000, and 15,000,000 plus 900,000 is 15,900,000 dollars. Correct.

Step 3: remove the fixed general conditions

General conditions are a fixed 1,480,000 dollars. 15,000,000 minus 1,480,000 equals 13,520,000 dollars. That amount covers the trade packages plus the contractor's contingency.

Step 4: remove the contractor's contingency

Contingency is 4 percent of trade cost, so 13,520,000 dollars equals trade cost times 1.04. Divide: 13,520,000 divided by 1.04 equals 13,000,000 dollars. Contingency is therefore 520,000 dollars. Check: 13,000,000 plus 520,000 is 13,520,000; plus 1,480,000 is 15,000,000; times 1.06 is 15,900,000 dollars.

LayerDollars
Trade packages13,000,000
Contractor's contingency, 4 percent520,000
General conditions1,480,000
Subtotal, cost15,000,000
Fee and insurance, 6 percent900,000
Guaranteed maximum price15,900,000

The bottom line of the reverse engineering: every trade package together must be bought for 13,000,000 dollars or less. Allocate that across packages from your estimate, and you have a buyout target for each one before a single bid arrives.

Say that out loud now.

Divide out the percentages, subtract the fixed costs, divide out the contingency. What is left is the trade budget I must defend.

Step 5: level three bids for one package

The concrete package has a buyout target of 3,300,000 dollars. Three prequalified bids arrive.

Bid A: 3,100,000 dollars, but it excludes placing the reinforcing steel and excludes winter protection. Quincy prices those exclusions at 180,000 and 60,000 dollars. Levelled: 3,100,000 plus 240,000 equals 3,340,000 dollars.

Bid B: 3,250,000 dollars, complete, but it includes concrete testing, which under this contract the owner buys separately from an independent laboratory. Remove that 40,000 dollars. Levelled: 3,250,000 minus 40,000 equals 3,210,000 dollars.

Bid C: 2,950,000 dollars, but it excludes pumping and hoisting, priced at 150,000 dollars; it qualifies its price as subject to cement price escalation without a cap, which Quincy values at a 120,000 dollar risk allowance; and it excludes its bond, priced at 45,000 dollars. Levelled: 2,950,000 plus 150,000 plus 120,000 plus 45,000 equals 3,265,000 dollars.

BidHeadlineAdjustmentsLevelled
A3,100,000plus 240,0003,340,000
B3,250,000minus 40,0003,210,000
C2,950,000plus 315,0003,265,000

The highest headline bid, B, is the lowest levelled price, at 3,210,000 dollars: 90,000 dollars under the 3,300,000 dollar target. The lowest headline bid, C, carries the most exclusions and an open-ended escalation qualification, and is really 55,000 dollars dearer than B before considering the risk that its escalation exposure is worse than the allowance.

Step 6: what to do with the 90,000 dollars

Record buyout variance of 90,000 dollars under target on concrete. Under a guaranteed maximum price, the contract decides whether that saving stays in the contractor's contingency, returns to the owner, or is shared. Hold it as protection until the remaining packages are bought, as Week 51 taught.

Step 7: test whether the cap is credible

The reverse calculation tells you what the trades may cost. Your own estimate tells you what they will probably cost. Compare them before you sign. Suppose your cost consultant's estimate of all trade packages, escalated to each package's midpoint, is 13,400,000 dollars. The cap only allows 13,000,000. The gap is 400,000 dollars, about 3 percent of trade cost, before a single bid is opened.

There are only four honest responses. Reduce scope or specification by 400,000 dollars through value engineering, priced and approved before the cap is signed. Accept a higher cap and test whether the pro forma still meets its return. Accept a thinner contractor's contingency, which moves risk back toward you. Or recognise that the deal does not work at this cap. What you must not do is sign a cap you believe is 400,000 dollars short and hope buyout closes the gap, because Week 51's arithmetic says that gap lands on your equity.

Reading the tabulation for warning signs

Before levelling, look at the spread. If four bids sit within a few percent of each other and one is 15 percent below the rest, the low bid is more likely to contain an error or a missing scope than a genius. Ask the bidder, in writing, to confirm its price against the numbered scope list. If it discovers a mistake, the tender rules from Day 4 decide whether it may withdraw. Awarding to a bidder who has mispriced the work buys you a contractor with a reason to recover its loss from you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing an exclusion too low, or not at all, so that a levelled bid looks cheap and the gap reappears as a change order. The control is to price each exclusion from your own estimate, not the bidder's, and to send every bidder the same clarification questions so the bids converge on the same scope.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner levels bids by asking each bidder whether it included an item, and accepts yes as the answer. Ask them to confirm in writing, against a numbered scope list, before award. The second beginner's mistake is to level only the price. Level the schedule too: a bid that needs ten more weeks for the package, on the critical path, costs the month-end interest and lost income Priya priced on Day 3, and that belongs on the sheet beside the dollars.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage reverse engineered a deal from public information to an implied land price. Today used the same discipline inward: from what the project can afford back to what each trade may cost. In both cases, working backward tells you the number you must defend before someone else names it for you.

Recap

From a 15,900,000 dollar cap: divide by 1.06 to remove fee and insurance, giving 15,000,000; subtract 1,480,000 of general conditions, giving 13,520,000; divide by 1.04 to remove contingency, giving a 13,000,000 dollar trade budget. Levelling three concrete bids turned the highest headline, B, into the lowest real price at 3,210,000 dollars.

Next: Marco on The Room: the scope interview with the low bidder, and the offer you must refuse.
checklist: I know the guaranteed maximum price my pro forma can afford before bids arrive.
I reverse engineer the cap into a trade budget and a target for each package.
I check every reverse calculation by running it forward again.
I price every exclusion and qualification from my own estimate.
I remove items from bids that the owner buys separately.
I send all bidders the same numbered clarification questions.
I record buyout variance for each package against its target.
head: Field checklist
speak: I work backward from what the project can afford. On a hypothetical guaranteed maximum price of 15,900,000 dollars, fee and insurance are 6 percent of cost, so I divide by 1.06 and get 15,000,000. I subtract fixed general conditions of 1,480,000 and get 13,520,000. The contractor's contingency is 4 percent of trade cost, so I divide by 1.04 and get a trade budget of 13,000,000 dollars, with 520,000 of contingency. Then I check it forward. Every package now has a buyout target. When three concrete bids arrive, I level them: bid A at 3,100,000 excluded reinforcing placement and winter protection, so it is really 3,340,000; bid B at 3,250,000 included testing the owner buys, so it is really 3,210,000; bid C at 2,950,000 excluded pumping and its bond and carried open escalation, so it is really 3,265,000. The highest headline bid is the lowest real price.
terms: Buyout target — the maximum amount allocated to a trade package before bids arrive, derived from the trade budget.
Exclusion — an item a bidder states it has not priced, which someone else must buy or the owner must accept as a gap.
Qualification — a condition a bidder attaches to its price, such as escalation not capped, which changes the risk in the bid.

hostile.q: Bid C is 300,000 dollars lower than the bid you chose. Why are you throwing that money away?
hostile.a: I am not. Levelled to the same scope, bid C is 3,265,000 dollars and our choice is 3,210,000. Bid C excludes pumping and hoisting and its bond, and carries open-ended cement escalation. Bid B is complete; we only removed testing, which we buy separately. The levelling sheet shows every adjustment and how each was priced from our estimate, and I will send it to you today.

title: The Scope Interview: Pinning Down the Low Bid, and Refusing the Offer
summary: A realistic post-bid interview with the preferred bidder for a structural package, where the owner must confirm scope line by line, resist a price-for-terms trade made in the room, and handle an improper personal offer. The lesson gives the lines to say and never to say, the question behind each question, when to stay silent, and closes with a monthly thread on ethics and anti-corruption in procurement.
body:
The scope interview is where a bid becomes a commitment. Walk the bidder through the scope one numbered line at a time, write down every answer, agree nothing in the room that is not on the list, and if anyone offers you something personal, end that part of the conversation at once.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause of the Wembley failure, as Ford framed it?

A. Treating a fixed price as a transfer of risk rather than a transfer of the cost of risk, on a unique structure with a developing design, so the risk stayed large and concentrated in a contractor whose losses drove disputes.

Q. In a schedule meeting, what is the right response to a promise that a slipping activity will be recovered?

A. Ask for the recovery plan in writing, with the resources, sequence and dates, and check it against the critical path, rather than accepting the promise.

Q. When you present a severe case to a lender, what should come with it?

A. The planned response: the trigger that would start it, the actions, the money available and who decides, so the lender sees a plan, not only a fear.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on Day 5 Quincy levelled three bids and found that the highest headline was the lowest real price. That conclusion rests on the bidder's scope being what you think it is. The interview is where you prove it. It is also where pressure, and sometimes temptation, arrives in person.

The scene

A meeting room, hypothetical. Present: you; Marco as your owner's representative; Quincy with the levelling sheet; and the estimator and a director from the preferred structural contractor, whose levelled bid is the lowest. On the table is a numbered scope list of forty items and the clarification questions every bidder received. You open.

"Thank you for the bid. You are our preferred bidder, subject to this meeting. We will go through the scope list one item at a time. For each one, I need a yes, a no, or an exclusion with its value. Quincy will record the answers, and at the end we will both initial the list. Nothing agreed here is final until it is in the written award."

That opening does three things: it tells the bidder it is winning, which lowers its guard and raises its willingness to commit; it sets a process; and it says that commitments live on paper, not in the room.

The lines to say

For every item: "Item 14, embedded plates for the curtain wall. Included, excluded or included with a qualification?" When the answer is vague: "So that I understand, if those plates are missing on site in month 9, whose cost is that?" When an exclusion appears: "Thank you. We have priced that at 35,000 dollars in our levelling. Do you agree with that figure, or would you like to include it at a price?" At the end: "Here is the list with your answers. Please initial each page. We will issue the letter of award on this basis."

Say that out loud now.

Included, excluded or qualified. Whose cost is it in month 9? Initial each page.

The lines never to say

Never say "You are the lowest bidder" before levelling is finished; you will hear "then we will not need to discuss exclusions." Never say "Another bidder can do it for less, can you match?"; that is bid shopping, it may breach tender duties in some jurisdictions, as LEX taught, and it signals that your tenders are not real. Never say "Don't worry, we'll sort that out later" about any item, because later is where the change order lives. Never accept a price reduction in exchange for a softer term, such as a reduced retainage or a waived bond, without pricing what you are giving away.

The question behind the question

The director says, "We could take 50,000 dollars off if you drop the performance bond." The question behind it may be, "Can we get this job without a surety looking at our balance sheet?" A contractor that wants to avoid a bond is sometimes telling you its surety is uncomfortable. Answer: "The bond stays. I would like to understand why removing it is worth 50,000 dollars to you."

The estimator asks, "Is the design going to change much?" The question behind it is, "How many change orders can we expect, and should we bid lower now and recover later?" Answer honestly and on the record: "The structural drawings are at issued-for-construction. Here is the list of open items. Price to the drawings."

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you ask whether an item is included. The bidder will often fill the pause with the real answer, including the qualification it hoped not to state. Stay silent after an exclusion is valued; let the bidder decide whether to include it. And stay silent, rather than reacting, if the director tries to take the conversation off the scope list.

The offer you must refuse

At the coffee break, the director mentions that his firm has a villa you could use over the holidays, or that his cousin could do some work at your house at cost. It is presented as friendliness. It is a personal benefit offered by a bidder during an award decision, and you must treat it as exactly that.

The line to say is short: "Thank you, but I cannot accept anything personal from a bidder or contractor. Let's get back to the scope." Then, after the meeting, write a short note to your file, and to your partners or lender if your agreements require it, recording what was offered and that you refused. If the offer was explicit or repeated, take advice on whether the firm should remain in the competition. Do not negotiate it, joke about it or leave it unanswered. An unanswered offer is often read as a deferred yes.

Monthly thread: ethics and anti-corruption in procurement

Procurement is where construction corruption usually lives, because it is where one person's decision moves large sums to one firm. The common forms are kickbacks, a share of the contract value returned to whoever influenced the award; bid rigging, where bidders agree among themselves who will win and at what price; and conflicts of interest, where the person evaluating bids has a hidden link to a bidder. Anti-bribery laws in many countries, including some that apply to conduct abroad, can make a developer liable for a bribe paid by its agents; the details vary by jurisdiction, so verify against the primary source before you rely on any of them.

The controls are simple and must be built before the first tender: a written gifts-and-hospitality rule that you follow yourself, a conflict-of-interest declaration signed by everyone who evaluates bids, at least two people on every evaluation, sealed or recorded bid opening, and a file note of every unusual approach. Rigged bids often show patterns: bids that are suspiciously close, the same firms always winning in rotation, or a losing bidder appearing later as a subcontractor to the winner. The question for you to answer, Mr Shabazz, is what you will write in your own gifts rule, and what you would do if the person making the offer were a friend.

Holding your state

A good bid interview is slow and dull, and that is a sign it is working. If you feel impatience to finish, that is when items get waved through. Keep the list in front of you and the pen moving. If the improper offer unsettles you, pause, say the refusal line, and return to the next number on the list; the structure carries you back to the work.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an award letter that refers to the bid but not to the clarified scope, so the exclusions you resolved in the room vanish. The control is an initialled scope list attached to and incorporated in the award.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner relaxes once the bidder is preferred and lets the interview become a friendly chat. Friendly is fine. Unrecorded is not.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught reciprocity: people feel obliged to return a favour, which is why a gift creates pressure even when nothing is asked in return. The villa offer is reciprocity used as a tool. Recognising the mechanism is what lets you refuse it calmly, without having to decide in the moment whether the person meant harm.

Recap

Walk the scope list item by item, record and initial every answer, and incorporate it into the award. Refuse trades of price for softer terms unless priced, never shop bids, stay silent after each question, and refuse any personal benefit at once and in writing.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair reading a bid tabulation and award recommendation.
checklist: I bring a numbered scope list and the clarification questions every bidder received.
I record included, excluded or qualified for every item, with a value for each exclusion.
I have the scope list initialled and incorporated into the award.
I never shop one bidder's price to another.
I price any concession on terms before I accept a price reduction for it.
I refuse any personal benefit from a bidder at once, and note it in writing.
Everyone who evaluates bids signs a conflict-of-interest declaration.
At least two people take part in every bid evaluation.
head: Field checklist
speak: The scope interview turns a bid into a commitment. I bring a numbered scope list and walk the preferred bidder through it line by line: included, excluded or qualified, and if excluded, at what value. When an answer is vague, I ask whose cost it is if the item is missing on site in month 9. At the end, the bidder initials every page and the list is attached to the award. I never shop prices between bidders, and I never trade a price cut for a softer term, like dropping the bond, without pricing what I am giving away; a contractor that wants to avoid a bond may be telling me something about its surety. I stay silent after each question. And if a bidder offers anything personal, a holiday, cheap work at my house, I refuse at once, return to the list, and write a note to the file. Corruption in construction lives in procurement, so my controls are built before the first tender.
terms: Kickback — a secret payment or benefit returned to a person who influenced a contract award, taken from the value of that contract.
Bid rigging — an agreement among bidders about who will win and at what price, instead of genuine competition.
Conflict-of-interest declaration — a signed statement by an evaluator disclosing any link to a bidder before bids are assessed.

hostile.q: Your preferred bidder's director has a family connection to your site superintendent. Why should your investors believe this award was fair?
hostile.a: Because the award was not decided by the superintendent. Everyone who evaluated the bids signed a conflict-of-interest declaration; the superintendent declared the connection and took no part. The evaluation was done by two people against written criteria, the levelling sheet shows every adjustment, and the scope list is initialled and attached. I will give the investors the declarations and the evaluation file, and if they want an independent review of the award, I will commission one.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 52 Review: Methods, Forms, Tenders and the Levelled Bid
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas on procurement: delivery methods, the FIDIC forms, Rule 52, the price of time, tender law and reverse engineering a guaranteed maximum price. Because week 52 is a fourth week, Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read a hypothetical bid tabulation and award recommendation as a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: decide who should carry each risk, choose the method and form that put it there, and then buy each package on levelled, documented, honestly evaluated bids.

Recall

Q. In a guaranteed maximum price, why might a fee stated as a percentage of cost be converted to a fixed fee?

A. Because a percentage fee grows when cost grows, rewarding change orders rather than savings. A fixed fee, adjusted only for owner-approved scope changes, points the incentive the right way.

Q. What does a look-ahead schedule do that the baseline does not?

A. It plans the next few weeks of work in field detail, so crews, materials and information are ready, while the baseline remains the approved plan that progress is measured against.

Q. What is a trigger in a stress-test response plan?

A. A measured value, agreed in advance, that starts a planned action, such as a coverage ratio or a cost variance crossing a stated level.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, procurement decisions are made once and paid for for years. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can sit across from a contractor, a lender's monitor or your own cost consultant and know which risks you are buying. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four delivery methods and who carries cost risk in each.

Answer: Design-bid-build: the contractor, on a fixed price for a finished design, while the owner warrants the design. Design-build: the design-builder, often fixed price against the owner's requirements. Construction manager at risk: the construction manager, above a guaranteed maximum price, except for owner changes. Construction manager as agent: the owner, who holds the trade contracts.

Question 2. Roughly, how do FIDIC's Red, Yellow and Silver books differ?

Answer: Red is for an employer's design, usually paid on measured quantities. Yellow is for a contractor's design to the employer's requirements. Silver is turnkey: the contractor designs and carries most of the design and much of the ground risk at a fixed price.

Question 3. State Rule 52.

Answer: Never treat a fixed price as risk gone; award it only to a contractor whose finances can carry the risk transferred, on a design mature enough to price, with approval and step-in rights over the critical subcontracts.

Question 4. On the week's hypothetical loan, what did one month at the end of construction cost?

Answer: About 241,667 dollars: about 116,667 dollars of interest on a 20,000,000 dollar loan at 7 percent, plus 125,000 dollars of net income not yet earned.

Question 5. What is Contract A, and what did M.J.B. Enterprises add?

Answer: In Canadian tender law, the preliminary contract formed with each compliant bidder when a formal tender is submitted, from Ron Engineering in 1981. M.J.B. Enterprises in 1999 held that the owner could not accept a non-compliant bid, despite a clause saying the lowest bid would not necessarily be accepted.

Question 6. From a 15,900,000 dollar cap with 6 percent fee and insurance, 1,480,000 dollars of general conditions and 4 percent contingency, what is the trade budget?

Answer: Divide by 1.06 to get 15,000,000; subtract 1,480,000 to get 13,520,000; divide by 1.04 to get 13,000,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Marco set out the four delivery methods, the FIDIC forms, prequalification, levelling and buyout. Ford and Cole took Wembley Stadium, where a fixed price moved cost but not consequences, giving Rule 52. Priya priced certainty and time, and showed that on most loans the month at the end is the most expensive one. LEX covered Contract A, the duties of a fair tender and how the standard forms allocate design and ground risk. Quincy worked backward from a guaranteed maximum price to a trade budget and levelled three bids. Marco ran the scope interview and the offer you must refuse.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 52 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical award recommendation as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Award Recommendation, Concrete Package. Bids received: A 3,100,000; B 3,250,000; C 2,950,000; D received one day after the deadline at 2,880,000. Recommendation: award to D at 2,880,000, the lowest price, as D has confirmed it will match all scope. Bid C was invited to revise after D's price was shared and declined. Levelling: not required as bids are broadly similar. Bond: waived for D in exchange for a 30,000 dollar reduction. Evaluation by: Site Superintendent. Conflicts: none known. D's director is a long-standing friend of the superintendent and has offered site office furniture free of charge.

The defects. First, bid D was late; accepting a bid received after the deadline breaches the tender's own rules and, in some jurisdictions, duties owed to the compliant bidders. Second, D's confirmation that it will match all scope is oral and unrecorded; there is no initialled scope list. Third, sharing D's price with C to invite a revision is bid shopping. Fourth, the claim that levelling is not required contradicts Day 5, where levelling reversed the ranking. Fifth, waiving the bond for 30,000 dollars removes security on a multi-million-dollar package for a trivial saving, with no analysis. Sixth, one person evaluated the bids, and that person has a declared friendship with the recommended bidder, which the "conflicts: none known" line directly contradicts. Seventh, free furniture from a bidder during the award is a personal benefit to the project team that must be refused and recorded, and its appearance here should trigger a review of the whole award.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence that should exist: the tender documents with the deadline and mandatory requirements; the bid opening record with times received; the levelling sheet; the initialled scope list; the signed conflict-of-interest declarations; the names of at least two evaluators; and the file note of the furniture offer and its refusal. An award that cannot produce these in an hour was decided before it was evaluated.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "How did you choose the contractor, and what happens if it goes wrong?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "We started with a risk table: who should carry design, ground, prices and delay. That pointed to a construction manager at risk with a guaranteed maximum price, so we keep design control, start earlier, and give the lender a firm cap. We prequalified every bidder on finances, bonding and safety, and levelled every bid to the same scope, which in one package turned the highest headline into the lowest real price. We worked backward from the cap to a trade budget for every package. The tender rules were written and followed, the scope is initialled and attached to each award, and two people evaluated each package with conflicts declared. If it goes wrong, the fixed cap moves the cost, but not the delay, so we hold a bond, approve the critical subcontractors, have step-in rights and keep our own contingency outside the contract."

Score your own answer before comparing. Did you open with the risk table? Did you name the method and why? Did you mention levelling, the cap and Rule 52? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is an award process that looks competitive but is not: late bids accepted, prices shared, one evaluator, no record. The control is written tender rules followed exactly, two evaluators, declared conflicts and a complete evaluation file.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing the delivery method because the contractor proposed it. Choose it from your own risk table, then invite contractors to that method.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught that a file which cannot show what advice was given, and when, is a file that cannot defend a decision. The award file is the procurement version: the auditor does not ask whether your choice was good, but whether you can prove it was fair.

Recap

Match the method to the risks, the form to the design responsibility and the contractor to the risk it can carry. Level every bid, reverse engineer every cap and record every award. Rule 52 keeps a fixed price from being mistaken for risk gone.

head: The six questions
speak: Procurement decides who carries each risk, so I start with a risk table, not a contractor. Design-bid-build fixes a price on a finished design and I warrant the design. Design-build buys both together against my requirements. Construction manager at risk advises during design and commits to a guaranteed maximum price. Construction manager as agent advises while I carry cost. FIDIC's Red, Yellow and Silver books move design and ground risk progressively to the contractor. On most loans, time is worth more than the premium for certainty: a month at the end can cost interest plus lost income. In Canada, a formal tender can create Contract A with every compliant bidder, so I write clear rules and follow them. I work backward from the cap to a trade budget, level every bid to the same scope, initial the scope list, and keep two evaluators with declared conflicts. Rule 52: a fixed price is never risk gone.
terms: Award recommendation — the written proposal to award a package to a named bidder, with the evaluation that supports it.
Bid opening record — the dated record of when each bid was received and opened, which proves compliance with the deadline.
Evaluation file — the complete set of documents behind an award: tender rules, bids, levelling, scope list, declarations and approvals.

hostile.q: Your award went to a late bidder, after its price was shown to a competitor, evaluated by one person who is its director's friend. Why shouldn't I report this to your lender?
hostile.a: You should not have to; I will tell the lender myself. That award should not stand. I am suspending it today, commissioning an independent review of the evaluation, and re-running the package under the original tender rules with two evaluators, signed conflict declarations and a levelled sheet. The furniture offer has been refused and recorded. You will have the review's findings and the re-run award file.
